content: Abdominal decompression was originally developed as a method to alleviate pain during labor. It has also been applied in cases of pregnancy complications and in healthy pregnant women to potentially enhance fetal well-being and intellectual development. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effects of antenatal abdominal decompression on perinatal outcomes, specifically in cases of maternal hypertension or impaired fetal growth. The review utilized the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register as of February 2, 2012, to identify relevant studies. The inclusion criteria were randomized or quasi-randomized trials comparing abdominal decompression with no decompression in women diagnosed with pre-eclampsia or in cases where the fetus was suspected to be compromised. One review author assessed the eligibility and quality of the trials. Three studies were included in the analysis, but all were noted to have a significant risk of bias. Therapeutic abdominal decompression was associated with several reductions in adverse outcomes. These included: A 64% reduction in persistent pre-eclampsia (relative risk 0.36, 95% confidence interval 0.18 to 0.72). A 63% reduction in fetal distress during labor (relative risk 0.37, 95% confidence interval 0.19 to 0.71). A 50% reduction in the likelihood of low birthweight (relative risk 0.50, 95% confidence interval 0.40 to 0.63). A 74% reduction in the risk of Apgar scores below six at one minute (relative risk 0.26, 95% confidence interval 0.12 to 0.56). A 61% reduction in perinatal mortality (relative risk 0.39, 95% confidence interval 0.22 to 0.71). However, the authors concluded that due to the methodological limitations of the included studies, the effects of therapeutic abdominal decompression remain unclear. The observed improvements in birthweight and perinatal mortality suggest that further research is warranted, particularly in cases of impaired fetal growth and potentially for women with pre-eclampsia.
